original_question: Let A \subset \mathbb{R}^d be a bounded set (not assumed closed). Consider the optimization problem: find a set S such that H^1(S) is minimal among all sets with S \cup A connected. Is it possible that this problem has no solution for some bounded A \subset \mathbb{R}^d, i.e., that the infimum of H^1(S) over admissible S is not attained? (Equivalently, is the closedness assumption on A necessary for solvability in this formulation?)
target_in_paper: Question 2.3 in Section 2.1 ("Uniqueness and existence"): "Is it possible to find a bounded set A such that the problem: ‘find S such that H^1(S) is minimal among all sets for which S \cup A is connected’ does not have a solution?"
correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper’s exact target. It correctly identifies the Steiner-type variational problem, keeps the input set A merely bounded rather than compact/closed, uses the correct connectivity constraint S \cup A connected, and correctly interprets "has no solution" as nonattainment of the infimum of H^1 over admissible sets. It also captures the author’s stated motivation that this asks whether the closedness assumption on A is really needed for solvability.
missing_details: To make the question fully stand-alone, it should explicitly say that H^1 denotes the one-dimensional Hausdorff measure.

It should specify the admissible class as all subsets S \subset \mathbb{R}^d (or in some Euclidean space), since Question 2.3 itself does not impose an a priori closedness condition on S in the optimization statement.

The nearby context should be included: just before Question 2.3, the paper recalls the standard compact-input Steiner-set problem, where for compact A one seeks a closed set S of minimal H^1 with S \cup A connected, and existence is known in that compact case.

If written fully stand-alone, the Euclidean ambient-space quantifier should be explicit: the paper is working in Euclidean spaces, so one should ask whether there exists some dimension d and some bounded A \subset \mathbb{R}^d with this nonattainment phenomenon.

Your parenthetical "Equivalently" is slightly stronger than the paper’s wording. The paper states the closedness issue as Paolini’s motivation for Question 2.3, not as a separately proved equivalence.
refined_question: In the Steiner-set problem in Euclidean space, existence is known for compact input sets: if A \subset \mathbb{R}^d is compact, one seeks a closed set S of minimal one-dimensional Hausdorff measure \mathcal{H}^1(S) such that S \cup A is connected. Does there exist some Euclidean dimension d and some bounded set A \subset \mathbb{R}^d for which the variational problem inf\{\mathcal{H}^1(S): S \subset \mathbb{R}^d,\ S \cup A \text{ is connected}\} is not attained by any admissible set S?
justification: The draft is targeting the paper’s Steiner-tree existence question, specifically Question 2.3 in Section 2.1, not any of the maximal-distance-minimizer questions in Section 1. The opening paragraph of Section 2 gives the standard compact-input formulation and recalls existence there; Question 2.3 then asks whether one can find a bounded set A for which the corresponding minimization problem has no minimizer, and the following sentence explains that the point is to test whether assuming A closed is necessary. The refined version keeps that exact scope and wording, while adding only the minimal context and notation needed to make it mathematically self-contained and faithful to the paper.
